testName: ICT3621 · 2025 Summative Assessment 3 · structure practice (100 marks)
sourceType: Source-verified 2025 assessment structure. The original municipal case rows are replaced with a clean equivalent relation while preserving the assessed normalisation, ERD, data-quality and DBMS-choice skills.
sourceLimitations: The real assessment uses a Johannesburg water-maintenance table. To avoid reproducing the source table verbatim while keeping the same skills, this app uses an equivalent municipal maintenance relation with the same normalisation problems.

caseStudy.title: Municipal maintenance incidents
functionalDependencies: (IncidentID, RepairCode) is the composite key in the starting relation.
IncidentID -> IncidentDate, ProblemType, Detail, IncidentTime, AreaCode, Street, LocationType, InspectorID, InspectorName

questions.text: Using the incident relation below and the supplied dependencies, draw a dependency diagram for the relation in First Normal Form (1NF). Mark the composite key and show the partial and transitive dependencies.
questions.correctAnswer: The 1NF relation keeps atomic values and uses composite key (IncidentID, RepairCode). Show IncidentID determining the incident attributes; RepairCode determining RepairDescription and RepairDate; IncidentID -> AreaCode -> AreaName, Region as a transitive dependency; and IncidentID -> InspectorID -> InspectorName as another transitive dependency.
aiRubric: Marks IncidentID + RepairCode as composite key.
questions.explanation:
1NF makes the values atomic but still allows redundancy caused by partial and transitive dependencies.

Student note: First identify the key, then draw arrows for every determinant before deciding which normal form is broken.

questions.text: Transform the design to Second Normal Form (2NF) and draw the resulting relations. Remove partial dependencies but leave transitive dependencies for the next step.
questions.correctAnswer: A valid 2NF design separates INCIDENT(IncidentID, incident details including AreaCode, AreaName, Region, InspectorID, InspectorName), REPAIR(RepairCode, RepairDescription, RepairDate) and INCIDENT_REPAIR(IncidentID, RepairCode). The bridge keeps the original many-to-many combination. Area and inspector transitive dependencies may still remain in INCIDENT at 2NF.
aiRubric: Removes attributes depending only on IncidentID from the composite-key relation.
Creates a bridge for IncidentID and RepairCode.
Does not incorrectly require transitive-dependency removal at 2NF.
questions.explanation:
2NF removes dependencies on only part of a composite key.

Student note: 2NF = 1NF plus no partial dependency.

questions.text: Transform the 2NF design to Third Normal Form (3NF). Draw the final relations and show primary and foreign keys.
questions.correctAnswer: A valid 3NF design is INCIDENT(IncidentID PK, IncidentDate, ProblemType, Detail, IncidentTime, AreaCode FK, Street, LocationType, InspectorID FK); AREA(AreaCode PK, AreaName, Region); INSPECTOR(InspectorID PK, InspectorName); REPAIR(RepairCode PK, RepairDescription, RepairDate); INCIDENT_REPAIR(IncidentID PK/FK, RepairCode PK/FK).
aiRubric: Creates AREA and removes AreaName/Region from INCIDENT.
Creates INSPECTOR and removes InspectorName from INCIDENT.
questions.explanation:
3NF removes transitive dependencies, so descriptive data about an area or inspector belongs in its own entity.

Student note: If a non-key field determines another non-key field, you probably still have a 3NF problem.

questions.text: Write five business rules that match your 3NF municipal-maintenance design.
questions.correctAnswer: Examples: one area can have many incidents and each incident occurs in one area; one inspector can handle many incidents and each incident references one inspector; one incident can require many repairs and one repair type can be used for many incidents through INCIDENT_REPAIR; each area code identifies one area; each inspector ID identifies one inspector. Equivalent consistent rules are acceptable.
aiRubric: Rules are business statements rather than SQL.
questions.explanation:
Business rules explain the real-world meaning behind the relationships and cardinalities.

Student note: Write rules using one/many and must/may so the cardinality can be drawn from the sentence.

questions.text: Draw an ERD for your 3NF relations. Include primary keys, foreign keys and cardinalities consistent with your business rules.
questions.correctAnswer: Expected core entities are INCIDENT, AREA, INSPECTOR, REPAIR and INCIDENT_REPAIR. AREA 1:M INCIDENT; INSPECTOR 1:M INCIDENT; INCIDENT and REPAIR are M:N resolved through INCIDENT_REPAIR. PKs/FKs and consistent cardinalities must be visible.
aiRubric: M:N incident/repair relationship resolved through bridge.
questions.explanation:
The ERD should be the visual form of the same rules and normalised relations you already created.

Student note: If the ERD contradicts your business rules, one of them still needs fixing.

questions.text: Discuss how a municipal organisation can keep operational database information accurate and reliable while still giving different users the information they need for their work and decisions.
questions.correctAnswer: Use validation and database constraints, controlled transaction processing, referential integrity, duplicate prevention, data-quality checks and correction procedures, role-based access/least privilege, views for different user groups, authentication, audit logs, backups and tested recovery, concurrency controls, clear ownership/stewardship, regular reconciliation, and timely update procedures. Access should match job needs without allowing uncontrolled modification.
questions.explanation:
Availability is not enough. Users need data that is correct, current and protected from accidental or unauthorised change.

Student note: Structure a 25-mark answer under Accuracy, Access, Protection and Recovery.

questions.text: A municipality must choose between an open-source DBMS and a proprietary DBMS. Recommend one approach for this scenario and justify the choice. A well-supported recommendation for either approach may earn full credit.
questions.correctAnswer: Either choice can be defensible. A strong answer compares total cost, licensing, vendor support, skills availability, security patching, reliability, ecosystem/tooling, integration, performance/scalability, compliance/governance, lock-in and long-term maintainability. The recommendation must connect those factors to the municipality's needs rather than claiming one category is always superior.
aiRubric: Connects reasons to the municipal scenario.
Does not claim an unsupported universal winner.
questions.explanation:
The question is a decision argument, not a definition exercise. Both open-source and proprietary systems have trade-offs.

Student note: State your choice, then defend it with criteria that matter to the organisation.
